column1: In a MIDI status byte, how are status bytes and data bytes distinguished at the bit level?
column2: Status bytes always have bit 7 set high (0x80–0xFF); data bytes always have bit 7 clear (0x00–0x7F). This single-bit sentinel lets receivers resynchronize after errors without out-of-band signaling.

column1: Decode the status byte 0x92. What message and channel does it represent?
column2: Note On, Channel 3 (0x90 base + offset 2). The wire protocol indexes channels from 0, but human interfaces label them from 1.

column1: Why does MIDI have no acknowledgment, flow control, or retransmission mechanism?
column2: MIDI operates as a unidirectional broadcast bus designed under severe hardware constraints—early synthesizers lacked the memory/CPU for stateful connection management, so senders simply transmit and trust correct decoding.

column1: What causes 'zipper noise' when sweeping a MIDI CC parameter slowly?
column2: CC values have only 7-bit resolution (128 steps, 0–127). A slow sweep (e.g., filter cutoff over 4 beats at 120 BPM) traverses discrete steps audibly, producing perceptible stepped artifacts in the modulated parameter.

column1: How does MIDI achieve 14-bit controller resolution despite 7-bit data bytes?
column2: By pairing two CC messages: CC 0–31 serve as MSB (coarse) controllers and their corresponding CC 32–63 serve as LSB (fine) partners, transmitted together to form a combined 14-bit value.

column1: What is the status byte format for a Control Change message, and what does 'n' represent?
column2: 0xBn, where n (0–15) encodes the MIDI channel. Each CC number is channel-specific, so CC 7 on channel 1 operates independently from CC 7 on channel 2.

column1: What is the PPQN resolution of MIDI Clock, and why was this value chosen?
column2: 24 pulses per quarter note. This provides exactly one tick per sixteenth-note triplet at any tempo, aligning with the rhythmic subdivisions most electronic instruments and sequencers use.

column1: How does a MIDI device infer tempo from MIDI Clock, given there is no explicit tempo message in MIDI 1.0?
column2: The receiving device measures the inter-arrival time between consecutive 0xF8 clock byte messages and infers current tempo implicitly from that clock rate.

column1: Name the three MIDI timing message types and the temporal problem each solves.
column2: MIDI Clock (0xF8) — beat-relative timing distribution; MTC/quarter-frame (0xF1) — absolute SMPTE timecode sync; Song Position Pointer (0xF2) — random-access repositioning within a sequence.

column1: In a Standard MIDI File, how is event timing encoded, and why is this significant?
column2: Each event carries a delta-time offset in abstract tick units (PPQN or SMPTE frames/sec) declared in the header chunk, not absolute clock time. This decouples musical content from playback tempo, allowing tempo changes without altering the recorded note data.

column1: What is the structural difference between SMF Type 0 and Type 1 files?
column2: Type 0 multiplexes all MIDI channels into a single interleaved track sorted by absolute time (for simple hardware sequencers); Type 1 maintains separate tracks for each musical part or channel.

column1: Why does MIDI transmit no data during held notes or silence, and what principle does this illustrate?
column2: MIDI follows event-driven sparsity: it transmits only state transitions (note-on/off, controller changes), not continuous audio samples. A held chord produces only the note-on and note-off bytes, generating zero traffic during sustain or silence.
